planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter or very early spring, or in fall in mild-winter regions for an overwintered crop.

directions: Sow seeds 1.5 to 2 inches deep directly in the garden while soil is still cool, spacing plants closely in blocks so they can support each other or provide staking for tall stems. This classic English heirloom is prized for its exceptional cold hardiness, tolerating hard frosts that would kill other legumes, making it a favorite for autumn sowing in mild climates or the earliest possible spring planting elsewhere. Pods grow long and fleshy, typically holding six to eight large, buttery-flavored beans that are excellent shelled fresh, dried for storage, or used in traditional Mediterranean and British dishes. Pinch out the growing tips once the first pods set to discourage aphids and encourage the plant to channel energy into pod development.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed well after the last frost, as this variety needs a long, warm growing season to mature its pods underground.

directions: Plant shelled, unroasted seeds about 1.5 inches deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil, since heavy clay makes it hard for pegs to penetrate and form pods. After yellow flowers fade, the plant sends down slender pegs that bury themselves and swell into pods, so hilling loose soil around the base at flowering time helps maximize pod set. Valencia is distinguished from other peanut types by clusters of three or four seeds per pod covered in a thin, bright reddish skin, and its notably sweet flavor makes it the classic choice for boiled peanuts across the South. Plants grow as an upright bunch rather than sprawling, so they fit well in raised beds and smaller garden rows.

planting.note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed, since seedlings are sensitive to cold, wet ground.

directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in rows or wide bands, inoculating with rhizobia bacteria if soybeans have not been grown in that bed before to boost nitrogen fixation and yields. Harvest whole pods while still bright green and plump but before the beans inside turn hard and yellow, usually indicated by pods filling out fully along the stem. This variety produces unusually large, sweet-flavored beans on tall, productive plants, making it a favorite among home gardeners who want bigger portions per pod than typical edamame types. Blanch or steam the harvested pods briefly and pop the beans free of the fuzzy pod before eating as a snack or adding to salads and stir-fries.

common_name: China Rose Radish (Rose China Winter Radish)

planting.note: Direct sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, since this radish is slower to mature and stores better than quick spring types.

directions: Sow seeds directly a half-inch deep and thin seedlings to a few inches apart, since crowded roots stay thin and pithy. Unlike fast-maturing spring radishes, this nineteenth-century heirloom is grown as a fall crop and left in the ground longer, forming a smooth, tapered root five to six inches long with rose-pink skin and crisp white flesh. Its flavor is notably more pungent than spring salad radishes, and its roots hold their quality in the ground or in cold storage well into winter, making it a traditional keeper variety for root cellars. Cool fall temperatures improve both texture and flavor, so avoid sowing it for a hot-weather harvest.

common_name: Sugar Sprint Pea (Sugar Sprint Snap Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring, since this pea thrives in cool weather and finishes before summer heat arrives.

directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in double rows along a low trellis or netting, since the compact vines benefit from light support even though they stay shorter than many climbing snap peas. This variety was bred for extra earliness and a concentrated harvest window, producing thick, crisp, stringless pods that are sweet enough to eat whole straight off the vine. Its shorter, sturdier vines make it a good choice for windy sites or gardeners who want snap peas without tall trellising, and it shows good tolerance to powdery mildew compared to older snap pea varieties. Pick pods promptly once they fill out to keep plants productive and pods tender.

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed, and make succession sowings every couple of weeks for a continuous harvest.

directions: Sow seeds an inch deep directly in the garden after soil has warmed, spacing plants close together in rows since compact bushy plants need little support. This dependable bush bean produces long, straight, round pods about five to six inches long that stay tender and stringless even when picked slightly larger than average. Vigorous, heavy-yielding plants tend to hold their pods up off the ground and above the foliage, which keeps them cleaner and makes for faster picking. It has long been a standard choice for home gardeners wanting a reliable, high-quality green bean for fresh eating, freezing, or canning.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed after the last frost, sowing in succession for continuous pods through summer.

directions: Plant seeds an inch deep directly in warm garden soil, thinning to a few inches apart so bushy plants have room to fill out without crowding. This long-popular bush bean produces slender, rounded, curved pods that are notably tender and stay stringless even at a fairly large size, giving gardeners a wider harvest window than many snap beans. Plants are heat tolerant and continue setting pods reliably through summer warmth, making this a dependable choice for extending the fresh bean harvest. Pick regularly to encourage continued flowering and pod set throughout the season.

scientific_name: Zea mays var. saccharata 'Golden Cross Bantam'

planting.note: Direct sow in blocks of at least four short rows after soil has warmed well past the last frost, since corn relies on wind pollination and needs neighboring plants to fill ears properly.

directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in blocks rather than single long rows to ensure reliable pollination, and side-dress with nitrogen once plants reach knee height. Introduced in the 1930s as one of the first widely grown hybrid sweet corns, this variety became a benchmark standard for decades thanks to its resistance to Stewart's wilt and its dependable yields of seven-inch ears filled with tender, golden-yellow kernels. Its classic old-fashioned sweet corn flavor, rather than the ultra-sugary taste of modern supersweet hybrids, still appeals to gardeners who remember it from earlier generations of home gardens. Harvest when kernels are plump and release a milky juice when pierced.

planting.note: Start seeds indoors under warmth and light a month or so before the last frost, then transplant out once nights stay reliably above 50 degrees.

directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant into warm soil after frost danger has passed, or direct sow once the garden has thoroughly warmed. Nufar was bred specifically to combine the classic large, glossy, sweet-scented leaves of Genovese basil with resistance to fusarium wilt, a soilborne disease that can devastate basil plantings, especially in beds where basil has been grown repeatedly. Its robust, upright plants hold up well through a full season of repeated pinching and harvesting for pesto and other Italian cooking. Regularly removing flower spikes keeps the plant leafier and extends its productive life into fall.

planting.note: Start seeds indoors early since leeks are slow to size up, then transplant seedlings into deep holes or trenches once they are pencil-thick and outdoor soil has warmed.

directions: Sow seeds indoors in flats or trays well ahead of the last frost, then transplant seedlings into holes or shallow trenches several inches deep so soil can be gradually mounded up around the stems to blanch them white as they grow. This classic French heirloom is known for its thick, broad blue-green leaves and unusually wide, well-blanched shaft, making it one of the largest and most substantial leeks commonly grown in home gardens. It has good cold tolerance and can often stay in the ground for a late fall or early winter harvest in milder climates, developing a mild, sweet flavor after light frost. Hill soil around the stems every few weeks through the growing season for the longest, whitest shafts.
